### From MHA and GQA to MLA, sparse attention, and hybrid architectures. Since it still hasn’t been released, I used the time to work on something that had been on my list for a while, namely, collecting, organizing, and refining the different LLM architectures I have covered over the past few years. So, over the last two weeks, I turned that effort into an LLM architecture gallery (with 45 entries at the time of this writing), which combines material from earlier articles with several important architectures I had not documented yet. So, in this article, I thought it would be interesting to recap all the recent attention variants that have been developed and used in prominent open-weight architectures in recent years. Multi-head attention (MHA) is the standard transformer version of that idea. It’s more meant as a quick overview to set the stage for related attention concepts like grouped-query attention, sliding window attention, and so on.

content.text:
Short answer: the *idea* of multiple heads is still completely standard. Every major LLM still uses multiple attention heads. What's changed is how the heads share their key/value projections, mostly to save memory at inference time.

The main lineage you should know:

Plain multi-head attention (MHA) gives every head its own Q, K, and V projections. That's the original, and it's expensive at inference because you cache K and V for every head across the whole sequence.

Multi-query attention (MQA) keeps many query heads but shares a *single* K and V across all of them. Much smaller KV cache, faster decoding, but a small quality hit.

Grouped-query attention (GQA) is the compromise that won: heads are split into groups, each group shares one K/V. It's basically a dial between MHA and MQA. This is what Llama 2/3, Mistral, and most current open models use.

Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is the newer one, from DeepSeek. Instead of just sharing K/V, it compresses them into a low-rank latent vector that gets cached, then reconstructed per head. Smaller cache than GQA while keeping closer to full-MHA quality.

The key thing to notice: all of these still have multiple *query* heads. None of them abandon the "multiple heads see different things" premise — they only economize on the K/V side, which is what dominates the inference memory cost.

Does the distinction between "why have multiple heads at all" versus "how to make them cheaper" make sense? If you want, I can go deeper on why MLA's compression doesn't destroy the per-head diversity — that's the subtle part.
